title: Global Resistance and the End of the Cold War
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: On the night of November 9, 1989, East German border guards opened the gates of the Berlin Wall, and ordinary Berliners poured through and began tearing it down. The wall had divided the city for twenty-eight years, and its fall symbolized the end of the Cold War in Europe.

Throughout the Cold War and decolonization era, ordinary people and popular movements resisted the power structures of their time — colonial rule, racial oppression, communist dictatorship, and the logic of the superpower blocs. This bottom-up dimension of human agency is essential to understanding the era.

In the United States, the Civil Rights Movement, led by figures like Martin Luther King Jr. and drawing directly on Gandhi's nonviolent methods, fought to dismantle legal segregation and win equal rights for African Americans.

In South Africa, the anti-apartheid movement, led by the African National Congress and figures like Nelson Mandela, waged a decades-long struggle against apartheid, a brutal system of legalized racial separation, finally triumphing in the early 1990s.

Within the Soviet bloc, dissidents and uprisings repeatedly challenged communist control: the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 and the Prague Spring in Czechoslovakia in 1968 were both crushed by Soviet tanks, showing the limits of resistance while the USSR was willing to use force.

Poland's Solidarity movement, a massive independent trade union led by Lech Walesa, defied the communist government throughout the 1980s and became the most successful popular challenge to communist rule in Eastern Europe before 1989.

On the global stage, the Non-Aligned Movement represented newly independent nations' collective resistance to being forced into either superpower camp, asserting an independent path in a bipolar world.

The common thread of the era's movements is human agency — the capacity of ordinary people, organizing together, to challenge even the most powerful states and systems. This theme connects every unit of the course, from peasant rebellions to anti-imperial revolts to twentieth-century freedom movements.

The most fundamental cause of the Cold War's end was the stagnation of the Soviet economy. The centrally planned communist system increasingly failed to match the West in producing consumer goods, innovation, or living standards, widening the gap between communist promises and grim reality.

The enormously expensive arms race and costly commitments like the disastrous war in Afghanistan (the USSR's 'Vietnam') drained resources the Soviet system could not spare, accelerating its economic crisis and contributing to its collapse.

Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev launched two famous reforms to save the failing system: perestroika ('restructuring' the economy) and glasnost ('openness,' relaxing censorship and allowing criticism). These reforms ultimately unleashed forces that brought the system down.

Crucially, Gorbachev signaled he would not use Soviet tanks to prop up the communist governments of Eastern Europe, as the USSR had done in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968. This removed the fear that had kept popular resistance in check.

Once people in Eastern Europe realized the Soviet army would not crush them, country after country — Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Romania — overthrew its communist government in 1989 in a largely peaceful chain of revolutions.

Germany reunified in 1990, and in 1991 the Soviet Union itself, wracked by economic crisis, nationalist movements among its many peoples, and collapsing ideological confidence, dissolved into fifteen independent states, leaving the United States as the world's sole superpower.

The interacting causes — economic stagnation, the costs of the arms race and Afghanistan, Gorbachev's reforms, and the surge of popular resistance — together brought down a superpower without a great-power war, one of the most remarkable outcomes in modern history.

The Indian independence and South African anti-apartheid struggles make a strong comparison: both were mass movements against European-rooted oppression led by global symbols (Gandhi, Mandela) using boycotts and civil disobedience, but India fought a colonial power ruling from abroad mostly nonviolently while South Africa confronted an entrenched home settler regime, requiring armed struggle and international sanctions.

Building a comparison argument requires choosing meaningful categories, stating specific similarities AND differences, and making a thesis that explains the comparison rather than just listing — for example, explaining why two decolonization or resistance movements followed different paths.

Continuity and change over time (CCOT) analysis establishes a 'before' baseline, identifies specific changes with evidence, identifies specific continuities, and explains the causes of change. Strong CCOT answers always address both change and continuity.

The Cold War and decolonization era shows major change — empires became nation-states and the world moved from multipolar to bipolar to a single superpower — alongside key continuities, especially the economic dependence (neo-colonialism) that persisted after political independence and ongoing great-power rivalry.

AP prompts signal their reasoning skill: 'compare' or 'similarities and differences' calls for comparison, while 'extent of change' or a span of dates calls for continuity and change over time. Identifying the skill first determines the whole structure of the essay.

The twentieth century opened with European empires dominating the globe and stumbling into two world wars, and closed with those empires gone, replaced by independent nations, and the bipolar Cold War order dissolved. The fall of the Berlin Wall symbolizes the end of this century of conflict and liberation, opening the era of globalization.
